newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election turns policy outlook upside down.
newsitem.headline: French election turns policy outlook upside down.

text.p: France's election was called to clear the way for bold new reforms on the way to monetary union.
But a surprise win by the combined left in the first round, the fall of Prime Minister Alain Juppe and threat of a crisis over Europe has turned the logic of the election upside down.
With Juppe's decision this week to step down as leader of the centre-right, the RPR-UDF ruling coalition has been left without a campaign platform ahead of Sunday's runoff vote.

On the left, the Socialist Party is toning down its campaign promises as it scents victory, with leader Lionel Jospin insisting repeatedly that it will introduce reforms gradually over the five-year normal lifetime of parliament.
"The closer Jospin is getting to power the less the left is promising," Daiwa Research Institute economist Bernard Godement said.

On the key issue of where they stand on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the centre-right has replaced the Socialists in the eyes of some in the financial markets as potentially the bigger threat to the single currency project.
President Jacques Chirac, attempting to rally the centre-right in a television speech this week, said the ruling parties had got the message that French voters sent them last Sunday.
Austerity, meant to prepare France for EMU, is out.
Instead Chirac offered a blend of social protection and economic liberalism.

The centre-right then put up two people to embody that promise -- socially-minded National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and former finance minister Alain Madelin, who wants deep tax cuts to get the economy moving again.
That, said one London-based economist, could be a recipe for cutting taxes while letting spending drift.
Seguin, who campaigned against the Maastricht Treaty in a 1992 referendum, has said he wants a softer approach to EMU, though he says he will honour the referendum vote in favour.

The Socialist Party, which like Chirac in his own 1995 presidential election campaign has promised to make jobs the priority, is now warning that it will do nothing until it sees the state of public finances.
Jospin repeated on Thursday his commitment to monetary union, and few believe he will risk the project founded by a Socialist government by letting spending run out of control.
In the meantime, a row in Germany over central bank gold may make it all the harder for a Socialist-led government to rock the boat too much on EMU for fear of capsizing it.

Jospin has already said that the party's conditions for EMU -- which include a European "economic government" and flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty -- are not "take it or leave it" conditions but the basis for discussion.
That said, though, the party has also promised not to do the same as Chirac, who changed policy five months after his election to make deficit reduction, and Europe, the priority.
"They are going to have to do something," Godement said.
"The Socialists are a bit trapped by their programme," Smith Barney economist Stephen Englander said.
"Even though in six months they will be walking away from it, they can't be seen to be walking away from it," he said.

For the Socialists, a key factor will be whether they can win on Sunday the 289 seats needed for an absolute majority -- or whether they have to share power with others on the left, including the Communist party.
Aside from the approach to Europe, other policy options remain unclear.

The Socialists originally said they would oppose new privatisations and would halt the partial sale, due next month, of France Telecom. Jospin has since said that staff would be consulted before any decision.

But even on the right, the departure of Juppe and his possible replacement by Seguin, combined with expected change at the Finance Ministry, has left the centre-right's policy on state sales less clear.
Seguin has made few policy comments, saying only that there are some "good things" in the original programme.
"The programmes are a reference. But everyone knows I have my own views which I hold by," he said on Thursday.
He, like Jospin, has also suggested reforms should be carried out over time.
"It is not in 40, in 50 or 60 days that you can judge...a new government," Seguin told French radio. "You have to take the time it needs."
